statutory.question: Does the conduct described fall within 5318(g)?
statutory.answer: Neutral — 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) suspicious activity reporting requirements may be implicated, but the facts do not show whether a covered U.S. financial institution was involved or whether any SAR filing obligation was triggered.
statutory.label: neutral
statutory.reasoning: 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) authorizes/mandates suspicious activity reporting by a “financial institution” (as defined under the BSA framework) when the institution detects a “suspicious transaction relevant to a possible violation of law or regulation,” and it also provides confidentiality/safe-harbor protections tied to such reports. Here, the fact pattern shows a Switzerland-incorporated business with expected monthly volume ~$52,531 sending three large, round-number outbound wires ($250,000; $2,500,000; $2,500,000) to counterparties including BVI and Delaware, which could be suspicious relative to the stated profile. However, § 5318(g) applies to the reporting obligations of the covered financial institution (e.g., a bank/MSB) handling the transactions, not directly to the customer’s conduct, and the facts do not identify (i) whether any U.S.-regulated “financial institution” processed these wires, (ii) whether the institution detected facts meeting the regulatory SAR triggers, or (iii) whether a SAR was required/failed to be filed. Therefore, § 5318(g) suspicious activity reporting requirements cannot be determined to clearly apply or not apply on these facts.
